12-018.r: Official poverty lines differ across States because price levels vary from State to State (inter-state price differentials in the Tendulkar poverty line basket).

12-019.r: Planning Commission poverty line 2011-12 (Tendulkar method): rural Rs. 816 per month (about Rs. 26 per day); urban Rs. 1000 per month (about Rs. 32 per day).
12-019.t: Don't swap them: Rs. 32 per day is the urban line, not rural; Rs. 42 is not an official line.

12-020.r: NSS 68th round (2011-12, Tendulkar method): poverty line Rs. 27.20/day rural, Rs. 33.33/day urban; 21.9% below poverty line, not 33.35%.
12-020.h: Rs. 816 and Rs. 1000 per month divided by a 30-day month give 27.20 and 33.33.

12-021.r: C. Rangarajan Committee (set up 2012, report June 2014) → poverty line Rs. 32/day per person rural, Rs. 47/day urban; separate rural and urban consumption baskets.

12-022.r: Lorenz curve → measures inequality of income (Max O. Lorenz, 1905); the 45° straight line = perfectly equal distribution; the more the curve sags, the more inequality.

12-023.r: Lorenz Curve → measures distribution of income or wealth (inequality); developed by Dr. Max O. Lorenz in 1905.

12-024.r: Gini coefficient (Corrado Gini) → measures income inequality; ranges 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality); derived from Lorenz curve; higher Gini = higher inequality.
12-024.h: Gini = Gap: bigger number, bigger gap between rich and poor.

12-025.r: 'Cultural Poverty' (Culture of Poverty) → Oscar Lewis, American anthropologist; poverty as a way of life passed on through generations.

12-026.r: 'Vicious Circle of Poverty' → Ragnar Nurkse, 'Problems of Capital Formation in Underdeveloped Countries' (1953); poor countries stay poor, trapped by demand- and supply-side forces.
hi: Vicious circle of poverty (गरीबी का दुष्चक्र)

12-027.r: Cyclic poor → those who keep shuffling between poor and non-poor; cyclical poverty is widespread but of limited duration (job loss, food scarcity, business cycle).

12-028.r: Poverty line in India fixed by the Planning Commission (nodal agency for national and State estimates); NITI Aayog replaced it from 1 January 2015.

12-030.r: Lakdawala Committee (1993) → poverty estimation: calorie-based consumption; State-specific poverty lines updated by CPI-IW (urban) and CPI-AL (rural); end 'scaling' to National Accounts.

12-031.r: Committees on poverty estimation → Suresh Tendulkar Committee and Lakdawala Committee (both correct); Vijay Kelkar and S.P. Gupta Committees are not.

12-032.r: Poverty-line committees: Alagh (1979), Lakdawala (1993), Tendulkar (2009), C. Rangarajan (2014); among the options, Lakdawala Committee's recommendations were used.
12-032.h: Order A-L-T-R: Alagh, Lakdawala, Tendulkar, Rangarajan.

12-033.r: Identifying urban BPL families → S.R. Hashim Expert Group (2010, Planning Commission); threefold test: residential, social and occupational vulnerability.
hi: Below Poverty Line (गरीबी रेखा से नीचे)

12-034.r: Treating people below poverty line as an identified group helps target poverty programmes: A and R true, R explains A.

12-035.r: In India both rich and poor are malnourished: rich eat wrong (over or unhealthy) diet, poor eat poor diet; A and R true, R explains A.

12-036.r: Tendulkar Committee: 37.2% below poverty line in 2004-05; by Tendulkar method (mixed reference period) 21.9% in 2011-12 (Planning Commission, July 2013).

12-038.r: Planning Commission (Tendulkar method): poverty fell 7.3 points, from 37.2% (2004-05) to 29.8% (about 30%) in 2009-10; data released 19 March 2012.

12-040.r: Planning Commission 2004-05 estimate (Uniform Recall Period) → 27.5% of Indians below the poverty line.

12-041.r: Planning Commission 1999-2000 estimate (Mixed Recall Period) → about 26% (26.1%) of Indian population below the poverty line.

12-042.r: Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007-2012) target → cut poverty head count ratio by 10 percentage points, with 7 crore new jobs; Twelfth Plan: 2 points per year.

12-043.r: World Development Report 2005 → 80% of India's population earned less than US$ 2 per day; World Bank: 12.9% below US$ 2.15/day in 2021.

12-044.r: FAO estimate (2003) → India had about 30% of the world's hungry; UN WFP now: about one-fourth of world's undernourished live in India.

12-045.r: Global Hunger Index 2017 (IFPRI) → India 100th of 119 countries; GHI 2022: 107th of 121; GHI 2023: 111th.

12-046.r: Global Hunger Index → 4 indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, child mortality (under five); created 2006 by IFPRI and Welthungerhilfe.

12-047.r: Government statistics of the nineties → poverty highest among Tribals of Bihar, Odisha, M.P. and Maharashtra.

12-048.r: NCAER survey (question period) → Bihar had the highest share below poverty line among given States; 2011-12 Planning Commission: Chhattisgarh highest (39.93%).

12-049.r: Bihar is backward due to income inequality, illiteracy, lack of industry and political will; regional disparity exists but is not the cause: A and R true, R not explanation.

12-050.r: Planning Commission 1999-2000 → highest poverty share in Odisha (47.1%); 2011-12 → most poor people in Uttar Pradesh (598.19 lakh), highest ratio Chhattisgarh (39.93%).
12-050.t: Don't confuse highest poverty ratio (percentage) with highest number of poor people (Uttar Pradesh).

12-052.r: Rajasthan 2011-12 (Tendulkar method, Planning Commission July 2013) → 14.71% (about 15%) below poverty line; 102.92 lakh poor.

12-053.r: Rangarajan poverty ratio 2011-12: All India 29.5%, Chhattisgarh 47.9% (not 37.9%), Goa 6.3%, Rajasthan 21.7%.

12-054.r: Lowest poverty ratio 2011-12 (Tendulkar): A&N Islands 1.00%, Lakshadweep, Goa 5.09%, Kerala 7.05%, Himachal Pradesh 8.06%, Sikkim, Punjab 8.26% → HP lowest among options.

12-055.r: Lowest poverty ratio among J&K, Punjab, Haryana and Goa → Goa (5.09%, Tendulkar method).

12-056.r: Least poverty among Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Kerala, Punjab → Kerala (19.6% in 2004-05; 7.05% in 2011-12, Tendulkar method).

12-057.r: World Bank: over 50% of India's poor lived in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha; 2011-12 most poor: UP (598.19 lakh), then Bihar, MP.

12-058.r: Poverty ratio 1993-94: Punjab 11.77%, Bihar 54.96% (about 55%), Uttar Pradesh 40.85%, Rajasthan 27.41%; none of the given pairs is correct.

12-060.r: Madhya Pradesh → 'Ethiopia of India' (India State Hunger Index 2008): excessive malnutrition and infant mortality like Ethiopia and Chad; A and R true, R explains A.

12-062.r: Ways to eradicate poverty → population control, increased savings (capital formation) and more investment in productive activities: all of these.

12-063.r: No clear picture of poverty extent (old Planning Commission and Tendulkar estimates differ); anti-poverty programmes restructured in nineties: A and R true, R not explanation.

12-064.r: DRDAs → secure inter-sectoral and inter-departmental coordination for anti-poverty programmes and watch effective use of their funds; they are not PRIs and do not run studies.

12-065.r: PDS started in the 1960s as a price support programme to give essential commodities at subsidised prices; food subsidy is provided by the Government of India, not States.

12-066.r: PDS aims → food security for the poor, prevent hoarding and black marketing, check exploitation by traders; also a tool of price stabilisation: all of the above.

12-067.r: Rural poverty eradication programmes: TRYSEM (15 August 1979), IRDP (2 October 1980), NREP (October 1980): all of the above.

12-068.r: Mitigating Poverty in Western Rajasthan (MPoWR) → financed by IFAD, Government of Rajasthan and Sir Ratan Tata Trust; six poorest blocks of Jodhpur division.

12-069.r: UNDP's two categories of poverty → Income poverty (lack of material necessities) and Human poverty (denial of opportunity for a decent life).

12-070.r: Human Poverty Index (HPI) → first published by UNDP in Human Development Report 1997; replaced by Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) from 2010.
12-070.h: HPI born 1997, retired 2010 when MPI took over.

12-071.r: HPI introduced in HDR 1997; replaced by Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) in 2010; MPI captures deprivations in health, education and living standards.

12-073.r: Multidimensional Poverty Index (OPHI with UNDP, 2010) → 3 dimensions (health, education, living standards) and 10 indicators.
12-073.h: 3 and 10: Health 2 + Education 2 + Living standards 6 indicators.

12-074.r: MPI dimensions → Health, Education and Living Standard (all three); developed in 2010 by OPHI and UNDP.

12-075.r: Best index to assess intensity of poverty in India → Multi-dimensional Poverty Index (first in HDR 2010), not HDI, GII or HPI.

12-076.r: MPI (OPHI with UNDP) covers household-level deprivation in education, health, assets and services; it does not cover PPP, budget deficit or GDP growth.

12-077.r: HDR 2013 → 53.7% of Indians in multidimensional poverty; HDR 2023/2024 → 16.4% (230.74 million, survey 2019-21).

12-078.r: To know if the rich get richer and the poor poorer → compare income distribution of an identical set of income receivers over different periods.

12-079.r: Causes of poverty → inadequate growth rate, high population growth, unemployment; an increasing rate of investment reduces poverty, so it is not a cause.

12-080.r: Social indicators of poverty → illiteracy, lack of healthcare, lack of jobs, malnutrition, no safe water or sanitation; fewer means of transport is not one.

12-081.r: Differential Interest Rate Scheme (1972) → concessional loans to weaker sections of society.

12-082.r: May 2013 Cabinet decision (under NRLM): women SHGs get loans up to Rs. 3 lakh at 7% interest (interest subvention).

12-083.r: 2008 Hoover Medal (announced 27 March 2009, New York) → Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, for upliftment of the poor and rural people.

12-084.r: Self-Help Groups and microfinance as a poverty tool → Muhammad Yunus (Bangladesh), founder of Grameen Bank, Nobel Peace Prize 2006.

12-085.r: SAARC Ministerial Conference on Poverty Alleviation → Islamabad, April 2002; 13th SAARC Summit (Dhaka 2005) declared 2006-2015 the SAARC Decade of Poverty Alleviation.

12-086.r: Main features of Indian social structure → excess rural population, many religions, many castes; poverty belongs to the socio-economic structure, not the social one.

12-087.r: Post-1991 rural economy (NITI Aayog, 2017): non-farm growth rose and rural employment growth fell; worker productivity rose in rural and urban areas; rural workforce share fell.

12-088.r: Growth rate of employment in India (question period) → about 2 percent per annum.
